transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Brushwood Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Infra Lead), Mateo Ruiz (Security Engineer)

Summary: Intro session to capture Brushwood's security gating criteria for inference deployments. Focus on compliance evidence, SSO and RBAC, KMS/BYOK, and retention requirements. Redwood to share SOC2 and architecture diagram, customer to share retention and PII list, and both to schedule pilot.

[00:00] Morgan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Morgan from Redwood. Can folks say where they're joining from?
[00:06] Aisha Khan: Hi, Aisha here in SF, head of ML at Brushwood.
[00:09] Tom Reynolds: Tom, infra lead in Boston.
[00:12] Mateo Ruiz: Mateo, security engineer, London.
[00:15] Diego Alvarez: Diego from Redwood, solutions engineering. I'll cover the more technical pieces today.
[00:22] Morgan Lee: Great, quick agenda — 1) understand your stack and threat model, 2) talk for each hosting mode (hosted, dedicated, private), 3) dive into key gates: SOC2/ISO, SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, KMS, retention — and capture next steps. Sound good?
[00:31] Aisha Khan: Yep, that works. We have an internal deadline — want to make a go/no-go decision by mid-September.
[00:35] Tom Reynolds: And procurement/security wants SOC2 evidence and an outline of how keys are handled.

[02:05] Diego Alvarez: Quick question on scale — what's your expected qps and typical sequence lengths? Helps with recommendations on whether dedicated pool is needed.
[02:12] Aisha Khan: For customer-facing conversational agents, peak is around 1k RPS across multiple endpoints. Avg sequence length about 250 tokens but can spike. Latency target is sub-400ms for tail p95.
[02:25] Diego Alvarez: Good context. Our dedicated pools are usually recommended above ~500 RPS steady or when you want pinned capacity and predictable p95. Hosted can handle that too, but dedicated gives pinning and SLA.

[04:10] Tom Reynolds: From a security perspective the big items are: a) SOC2 report, b) ability to use our KMS (BYOK), c) SSO with SAML and SCIM for provisioning, d) audit logs retained for 1 year and searchable, e) option for private VPC or on-prem.
[04:22] Morgan Lee: That's the checklist we expected. Quick callouts — we are SOC2 Type II and can share report; ISO 27001 is in our roadmap. For keys, we support both Redwood-managed KMS and BYOK integrations with major cloud KMS providers, and our private deployment supports customer-controlled HSM in the VPC path.

[06:00] Mateo Ruiz: When you say BYOK, you mean we can bring keys to the redwood-managed service and you never see them? How are they rotated and audited?
[06:08] Diego Alvarez: Yeah, great question. For hosted we do envelope encryption with customer KMS — the model artifacts at rest are encrypted with a data key that is wrapped by your KMS. Redwood doesn't retain the plaintext key. Keys can be rotated per your KMS policy. For private deployment, the keys live in your VPC HSM instance. Audit logs capture key usage events but the exact schema might vary by provider.
[06:30] Mateo Ruiz: And that's visible to us? We need to see key unwrap/wrap events.
[06:35] Diego Alvarez: You'd get audit events for key operations — we'll share the audit schema. There's sometimes a mapping between cloud KMS event names and what ends up in our log ingestion.

[08:10] Aisha Khan: On SSO, we use Okta and enforce SCIM provisioning and role mapping. We need RBAC aligned to our internal roles, and token expiry policies.
[08:20] Morgan Lee: We support SAML SSO and SCIM for user sync. RBAC is configurable — you can map groups from your IdP into Redwood roles (admin, viewer, deployer). Token TTLs can be set; we support short-lived tokens and session revocation.

[09:55] Tom Reynolds: Audit logs — our compliance requires that API-level audit logs are immutable and retained for at least 12 months, preferably 24 in some regions. Can those logs be exported to our SIEM?
[10:05] Diego Alvarez: Yes — logs can stream to your logging infrastructure (e.g., CloudWatch, Stackdriver, or a syslog endpoint). We also provide downloadable logs from the console and log forwarding for events (authn, authz, model calls, config changes). Retention windows vary by plan; Dedicated/Private have configurable retention.

[12:40] Mateo Ruiz: About data residency — we have EU customers and need tokenization and logs to stay in EU regions. Does Redwood host regional deployments?
[12:47] Morgan Lee: We have regional availability in EU and NA. For strict residency we recommend Private (VPC) or Dedicated in region — hosted has regional endpoints but data flow details depend on configuration. We'll share our region map.

[14:30] Aisha Khan: A practical question — if we go hosted initially, is there an easy migration path to Dedicated or Private later without retooling?
[14:37] Diego Alvarez: Yes — deployments are abstracted. You can pin model versions and rollout policies. We provide migration documents; in practice model artifacts, prompts, and traffic routing can be moved with minimal client-side change — usually a config switch and a key rotation if BYOK changes.

[16:20] Tom Reynolds: On the SOC2 doc — can we get the full report or just an attestation? Our procurement needs the full Type II for vendor risk assessment.
[16:28] Morgan Lee: We can share the SOC2 Type II under an NDA — we typically provide the report to security teams. I'll attach it to the follow-up email.

[18:05] Aisha Khan: For pilot success criteria — we'd want latency p95 < 400ms, correctness on a 500-sample prompt set (eval), and logging completeness for all inference calls. Can Redwood produce token-level cost breakdown for the pilot?
[18:18] Diego Alvarez: We do token-level cost and latency traces in the console. For pilot we'll instrument a route and share the breakdown per route and per token. We can also enable KV cache and batching profiles to improve unit cost.

[20:00] Mateo Ruiz: Two security nitpicks — 1) do you have a formal process for incident response and do you publish a runbook? 2) what's your timeline for ISO 27001?
[20:09] Morgan Lee: We have an IR process and will share a high level playbook and contacts. ISO 27001 target is H1 2027 — that's the current plan but I'll mark that as subject to change.

[22:40] Tom Reynolds: Logging retention is a hard requirement. If we choose hosted, what's the SLA around log availability and integrity? We need to ensure logs are not lost during rollouts.
[22:49] Diego Alvarez: For hosted we replicate logs across clusters and maintain a 99.9% availability SLA on log search for paid plans. For Dedicated, you have direct control and can set retention policies; Private gives you full ownership. We'll share the exact SLA numbers in the follow-up doc.

[25:00] Aisha Khan: Regarding RBAC, we have more granular roles — not just admin/deployer/viewer. Can we bring custom roles?
[25:07] Diego Alvarez: Yes, Dedicated and Private support custom roles and fine-grained permissions. Hosted has a set of predefined roles, but we can extend those for enterprise customers under a contract.

[27:10] Morgan Lee: Any questions on encryption at rest for model artifacts and in-flight?
[27:14] Mateo Ruiz: For in-flight we need TLS 1.2+ with mTLS option inside VPC.
[27:19] Diego Alvarez: TLS 1.2/1.3 is supported; mTLS for service-to-service inside VPC for Private is available. For hosted we support TLS and token-based auth; mTLS can be supported in dedicated/customer peering setups.

[29:40] Tom Reynolds: How do you handle audit of prompt logs — we have to redact PII or store hashed identifiers. Is there a native redaction/pseudonymization feature?
[29:48] Diego Alvarez: We have configurable redaction rules and field-level filtering before logs are persisted. There is also a callback/webhook option so you can push through your own redaction pipeline before storing.

[32:10] Aisha Khan: On retention policy — we need to retain inference logs for 12 months and training artifacts for 3 years; can Redwood support multiple retention classes?
[32:18] Diego Alvarez: In Dedicated/Private yes — you can set different retention buckets per asset type. Hosted can offer custom retention tiers for enterprise plans; otherwise there are default retention lengths. We'll include retention tiering options in the docs.

[34:00] Mateo Ruiz: Procurement also asked about background checks and SOC 3/ISO for marketing — not essential but nice.
[34:05] Morgan Lee: We publish a SOC3 summary publicly. ISO 27001 as mentioned is planned. We'll include links.

[36:20] Aisha Khan: Could you explain the 'fall back to compatible model variant when capacity constrained' — we don't want quality regressions mid-session.
[36:28] Diego Alvarez: Yes — policy-driven fallbacks are configurable. You can specify strictness: allow only same-family fallbacks (e.g., quantized variant of same model) or permit different quality tiers. Sessions can be pinned to a model family to avoid mid-conversation regressions. We'll show examples in the runbook.

[38:45] Tom Reynolds: About penetration testing — do you allow third-party pentests and what's the coordination?
[38:51] Morgan Lee: We do allow pentesting under a coordinated plan and an NDA; we have a process and point of contact. For Private it's simpler since it's in your environment.

[40:20] Diego Alvarez: For the pilot scope proposal — propose 2-week run, route 50% of production traffic for a small subset of customers, target 1k RPS spike tests, evaluate latency, cost, and logs. Does that align?
[40:31] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. We'll need a pilot contract addendum covering data handling and access controls.

[42:00] Morgan Lee: We'll draft a pilot SOW and include success criteria you outlined: p95 < 400ms, eval accuracy on 500-sample set, and complete audit logs.

[44:15] Mateo Ruiz: A couple more items — we need the schema for audit events so our SIEM team can map fields, and we want a sample of the retention/export API.
[44:24] Diego Alvarez: Noted — I'll attach: 1) audit event schema, 2) log export API docs, and 3) sample log export payload.

[46:40] Tom Reynolds: On the legal side, do you do data processing addenda (DPA) and subprocessor lists?
[46:47] Morgan Lee: Yes, we have a standard DPA and maintain a subprocessor list. We'll provide those during procurement.

[48:30] Aisha Khan: Any known limitations with Okta SCIM group sync we should be aware of?
[48:36] Diego Alvarez: SCIM support is full for user and group sync; some attribute mappings might need a custom transform. We'll work with your IdP team during onboarding.

[50:05] Morgan Lee: Alright I'll recap next steps — I'll send SOC2 and the architecture/region map; Diego will send the audit schema, export API, and pilot config; Brushwood will send retention policy and PII list. After doc review we'll schedule pilot kickoff (week of 2026-08-31). Any objections?
[50:20] Aisha Khan: No objections — thanks.
[50:23] Tom Reynolds: Sounds good.
[50:26] Mateo Ruiz: Fine with that.
[50:30] Morgan Lee: Great — I'll follow up with email. Thanks all.
[50:35] Diego Alvarez: Thanks everyone.
[50:40] End of recording.

Notes on transcription quality: medium — occasional mis-heard technical terms (e.g., "K V cash" for KV cache, "sammel" for SAML) and overlapping talk in a few segments.
